nameStory: Pelegrina flaviceps gets its scientific name from the Latin 'flavus' meaning yellow and 'ceps' meaning head, literally translating to 'yellow-head.' This tiny jumping spider earned its name from the distinctive yellowish coloration often found on its head region. The genus name Pelegrina honors the wandering nature of these spiders, much like pilgrims exploring new territories.
description: The Pelegrina flaviceps is a small jumping spider that calls the northeastern United States and southeastern Canada home. Like all jumping spiders, it has a compact, robust body with relatively short legs and large, forward-facing eyes that give it excellent vision for hunting. These spiders are tiny hunters, typically measuring just a few millimeters in length. They're active predators that stalk their prey rather than building webs to catch food.

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Four large eyes arranged in a square pattern on the front of the face, with the two center eyes noticeably larger and more prominent, giving them an almost cartoon-like appearance when viewed head-on

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Compact, chunky build with a relatively flat cephalothorax (front section) and short, sturdy legs that feel springy to the touch if gently handled

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Yellowish coloration on the head region, though this can vary in intensity and may appear more cream-colored or pale depending on the individual and lighting

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Very small spider, usually just 3-5 millimeters in body length - about the size of a match head or small peppercorn

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Moves in quick, jerky motions with sudden stops, often turning to face observers directly due to their excellent eyesight and curious nature

habitat: Look for Pelegrina flaviceps in wooded areas throughout New England, particularly on tree bark, fallen logs, and leaf litter in deciduous and mixed forests. They prefer areas with dappled sunlight where they can hunt for small insects among the forest debris. These spiders are often found at eye level on tree trunks or scurrying across sun-warmed rocks and wooden surfaces.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active as temperatures warm, emerging to hunt and beginning their mating displays with characteristic jumping spider courtship dances.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most commonly observed hunting during warm, sunny days. This is the best time to spot their distinctive yellowish head markings.
seasonality.fall: Adults continue hunting but begin preparing for winter, with females potentially carrying egg sacs in protected locations.
seasonality.winter: Adults typically overwinter in protected spaces under bark, in leaf litter, or other sheltered microhabitats, becoming dormant until spring.

funFact: Despite being smaller than your pinky nail, Pelegrina flaviceps has vision that's proportionally better than a cat's - they can spot movement and detail at distances up to 20 times their body length, making them incredibly efficient micro-predators in the forest understory.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other small Pelegrina jumping spiders, especially the Common white-cheeked jumping spider which shares similar habitats. Look for the yellowish head coloration in flaviceps versus the white facial markings in white-cheeked species - think 'butter versus cream' as a memory trick.
contextualKnowledge: The genus Pelegrina contains several very similar species that can be challenging to distinguish without close examination, and even experts sometimes need to examine specimens under magnification to be certain of identification in the field.
compareHints: Pelegrina flaviceps differs from its close relatives primarily in its yellowish head coloration - the Common white-cheeked jumping spider has distinctive white facial markings, while the Peppered Jumping Spider typically shows more mottled, salt-and-pepper patterning. The Yellowleg Jumping Spider, as its name suggests, has more prominent yellow coloration on the legs rather than concentrated on the head region.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Pelegrina relatives in New England, the white-cheeked jumping spider is distinguished by those prominent pale cheek markings - the peppered jumping spider has more scattered light spots, while the yellowleg jumping spider has distinctly yellow-colored legs.
